title: Automate Photoshop (2026 Guide)
summary: Automate Photoshop by recording your edits once as an Action, then run them on multiple files through File > Automate > Batch.
body_markdown:
## Record and Test an Action


Do the job by hand once, with the Actions panel capturing each step, and recording is finished. Testing's playing that action once on a single open image before you hand it a folder.


### Record the Action in the Actions panel


Open Window > Actions, click the new-action button at the bottom of the panel, and Photoshop asks for four things: Name, Set, Function Key and Color. Name and Set are housekeeping, since a set is just a folder for related actions.


You can skip Function Key and Color, but they matter later. A function key assigned here can collide with a shortcut you already use, and Color only shows up in Button Mode.


Click Record and the recording starts at once, so have the image open and the first move planned.


Then do the job once, deliberately, and click Stop. Menu commands, most selection and crop operations, and layer and adjustment changes record.


Brush strokes, tool options and view settings such as zoom don't, so a step you can see on screen may be missing from the list. Read the recorded steps in the panel before trusting them.


### Insert a Stop, a menu item or a path


Where recording leaves gaps, these three fill them. They're all in the Actions panel menu.


Two of the special commands need explaining. Insert Menu Item records a command that normally refuses to record: you choose it from the menu while the dialog is open, and the action calls it on playback.


Insert Path stores a path from the Paths panel so the action can recreate it on each image, which helps when the same outline applies to every file.


When a batch runs unattended, a stop's a hand-raise nobody answers. Insert Stop adds a message that pauses playback for a person, so use it while building and testing, then remove it before the real run.


### When a recorded action can't decide


Everything above's a straight line: the action does step one, then step two, in the same order on every file. A flow builder canvas, like the one shown here, makes the contrast plain.


It starts from a trigger (a new customer created in Tesorio, a finance platform) and runs a router that asks whether the name starts with A through L. The router sends the record down one of two assign steps before an End.


Where a recorded action can't decide what to do from the data in front of it, this flow does. If your job needs a decision per file, you've found one of the walls. If it doesn't, keep recording.


### Test the action on one image


Select the action, click Play Selection, and watch the History panel. Run it on a copy, not your only original.


If any step fails or does something unexpected, fix the action now, because a flaw repeated across a whole folder is far more expensive to find afterward.
